analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress from ever becoming lobbyists and tightly restricts the revolving door.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would impose a lifetime lobbying ban on former members of Congress, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote since it was introduced in May 2025 with 7 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime for any former member of Congress or elected congressional officer to ever lobby Congress after leaving office. It would extend the existing lobbying ban for senior congressional staff from 1 year to 6 years, bar registered lobbyists and foreign agents from working for members or committees they lobbied for 6 years, raise the maximum fine for violating lobbying disclosure rules from $200,000 to $500,000, and force large lobbying firms to publicly disclose every former congressional employee they hire on a searchable government website called lobbyists.gov. It was introduced by Rep. Joe Neguse (D-CO) in May 2025 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want laws written without the immediate influence of people who just left Congress and the lobbyists who once had access to their offices. Government watchdogs and transparency advocates also benefit from the proposed lobbyists.gov database, which would make it easy to see which lobbying firms hire which former congressional staff.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime, punishable under the existing criminal penalties of 18 U.S.C. 216, for a former Senator, Representative, or elected congressional officer to ever lobby Congress on anyone's behalf after leaving office [S2].
Extends the post-employment lobbying ban for congressional staff from 1 year to 6 years [S2].

Bars registered lobbyists and agents of foreign principals from being hired by a member or committee they lobbied within the previous 6 years, with an ethics-committee waiver only for 'compelling national need' [S2].

Requires firms with more than 3 registered lobbyists to report every former member or senior staffer they employ, and posts that list on a new searchable public database, lobbyists.gov, with filings copied to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to check for underreporting [S2].
Raises the maximum civil fine for violating the Lobbying Disclosure Act from $200,000 to $500,000 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and corporate influence shops lose access to the revolving door: they could no longer hire former members for life or recently-lobbied lobbyists for 6 years, would face steep fines for disclosure violations, and would have to publish their former-congressional-employee roster. Former members and senior staff would lose the most lucrative typical next step in their careers.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban could be challenged as overbroad, since lobbying is constitutionally protected activity and courts have historically struck down or narrowed blanket restrictions on former officials' employment; the bill offers no time-limited alternative for members [S2].

The ban on hiring registered lobbyists for 6 years could deprive congressional committees of subject-matter experts drawn from regulated industries, and the 'substantial lobbying contact' test is judgment-based, which could make enforcement inconsistent [S2].

The ethics-committee waiver for the lobbyist-hiring ban leaves an exception that an aggressive committee could use routinely, and enforcement depends on appropriations and on the D.C. U.S. Attorney's office actually policing filings [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — a lifetime member ban, longer staff cooling-off periods, and public disclosure of lobbying-firm hires — attack the most direct channel between past public office and paid influence, and the disclosure database is a genuine, cheap transparency gain. The real costs are practical: an untested lifetime ban faces legal risk, committees may lose qualified expertise, and the waiver and enforcement provisions could blunt the bill's effect. On balance the bill targets a concentrated interest's access rather than a public program, and its costs fall on the influence industry, not on ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has not scheduled a hearing or vote, so it is waiting and would die there if nothing changes before the Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the Close the Revolving Door Act of 2025 on May 21, 2025 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — the only action the bill has received [S4].
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican has signed on [S3].
As of the latest action record, the bill has had no committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or further referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the lobbying industry and former members of Congress: with the bill sitting without committee action, the current lobbying rules — a 1-year staff ban and no lifetime restriction on members — remain in force and the disclosure status quo is unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbyists and former members, for now

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee on May 21, 2025.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with authority to schedule hearings and markups
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it has sat in committee since referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Brought no such revolving-door measure to the floor in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 supporters (the sponsor plus 7 cosponsors) are House Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; the committee where the bill sits is chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and corporate influence shops
industries.note: The bill bars them from hiring former members for life and recently-lobbied lobbyists for 6 years, forces public disclosure of every former congressional employee on their payroll, and raises fines for disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000. Their business depends on the access the revolving door provides, so the bill's gain for transparency is their loss.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: Members and elected officers would face a lifetime criminal ban on lobbying Congress, and staff bans would stretch from 1 year to 6 years. This removes the most lucrative post-congressional career path, which is precisely the incentive the bill aims to eliminate.

industries.industry: Foreign agents lobbying on behalf of foreign principals
industries.note: The bill explicitly bars agents of foreign principals from congressional employment for 6 years after lobbying contacts and folds them into the new disclosure rules, closing a channel of foreign influence over legislation.

analysis.trajectory: Bills on congressional ethics and the revolving door routinely die in committee without a hearing, and this one has sat in the House Judiciary Committee for months with no Republican support and no floor action. Unless the committee schedules a markup or leadership decides to prioritize it, the bill will expire at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027.
